final_recommendation: The room converged on a narrow path: Mexico must deliver binding Protocol text by Wednesday noon with wage floors, 30-day audit triggers, and automatic day-31 tariff suspension ('shall suspend') language. Canada will ratify only if the Protocol is limited to labor enforcement and does not reopen dairy or Chapter 19. If Mexico delivers this text and Friday's cabinet letter, ratification passes with 40+ Democratic votes and business/labor support. If the text hedges or slips, the deal reopens or dies.
minority_objections: Mexico's concern that automatic tariffs and U.S. audit authority infringe sovereignty over domestic labor enforcement
Business lobby's initial worry that enforcement uncertainty would delay ratification, though later resolved by committing to support enforceable language
key_conflicts: U.S. Congress/labor demand for automatic day-31 tariffs ('shall suspend') vs. Mexico's sovereignty concern over U.S. override of domestic enforcement
Timing pressure: Congress demands Protocol draft by Wednesday noon vs. Mexico's need for domestic cabinet approval by Friday
Legal precision: 'may suspend' vs. 'shall suspend' language determining whether enforcement is real or discretionary
Canada's red line that Protocol must not reopen dairy or Chapter 19 vs. risk that any amendment could unravel the package
key_concessions: Mexico agreed to 30-day audit trigger and day-31 automatic tariff clock, abandoning initial 45-day domestic enforcement window
U.S. Democrats accepted Mexico retaining sovereignty over remedy process within the 30-day window, as long as tariffs are automatic on day 31
Business lobby shifted from opposing enforcement complexity to publicly supporting enforceable labor language to secure certainty
Canada accepted Protocol amendment limited to labor enforcement, abandoning resistance to any reopening
red_lines: U.S. Congress: Protocol text must contain 'shall suspend' automatic tariff language by Wednesday, not 'may suspend' discretionary authority
Labor union: No vote without binding wage floors, 30-day audit trigger, and day-31 tariff clock in legal text—no framework promises
Canada: Protocol must be limited to labor enforcement only; any attempt to reopen dairy, Chapter 19, or other chapters kills ratification
Mexico: Joint commission documents violations, but Mexico retains sovereignty over domestic remedy process within 30-day window
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Risk that Mexico's cabinet or Congress might reject automatic tariff language between Wednesday draft and Friday signature
Risk that 'shall suspend' language could be interpreted differently by U.S. and Mexican legal teams, creating post-ratification disputes
Risk that business lobby's public support statement Thursday could backfire if Mexico's draft disappoints, creating narrative whiplash
Risk that Canada's Parliament might reject the Protocol even if limited to labor, if domestic opposition frames it as U.S. dictating terms
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Mexico's legal team delivers 'shall suspend' vs. 'may suspend' language in Wednesday draft
Whether Mexico's cabinet actually signs Friday letter after seeing Congressional reaction to Wednesday draft
Whether Canada's Parliament accepts Protocol as sufficiently narrow or demands full renegotiation
Whether business lobby's Thursday statement moves swing votes or creates backlash if enforcement language is seen as too weak
Whether media narrative frames Wednesday draft as 'real enforcement' or 'loophole' based on legal precision
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved conditional convergence on a Wednesday-Friday timeline, but critical uncertainty remains: (1) whether Mexico's legal team will use 'shall suspend' automatic language or hedge with 'may suspend'; (2) whether Mexico's cabinet will actually sign Friday after Congressional/labor reaction to the draft; (3) whether the 30-day remedy window will be seen as real sovereignty protection or enforcement delay; (4) whether Canada's red line on Protocol scope will hold if any other issue surfaces in drafting. The deal's survival hinges on Mexico delivering binding, automatic enforcement language by Wednesday noon—any hedging or delay triggers reopening or collapse.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Dominated every round: 'my caucus walks,' 'this deal dies in committee,' 'no text by Wednesday, we reopen the whole deal'—ratification failure was the central threat driving all concessions.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Drove the entire negotiation: labor demanded 30-day audit, day-31 automatic tariffs, 'shall suspend' language, and threatened to pull endorsement publicly if text hedged—shaped every compromise.
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Genuinely developed: business shifted from opposing complexity to publicly supporting enforceable language to secure certainty, mobilized Roundtable statement—but not the dominant driver.
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Genuinely discussed: Canada's red line that Protocol must not reopen dairy/Chapter 19 was repeated and shaped Mexico's scope commitment—but secondary to labor enforcement pressure.
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Genuinely discussed: Mexico repeatedly insisted on retaining sovereignty over domestic remedy process, shaped the 30-day window compromise—but ultimately conceded automatic tariffs.
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Genuinely discussed: media framed Wednesday draft as the public test of 'real enforcement vs. shell game,' set narrative stakes—but did not drive the room's core decisions.
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Dominated the room: every participant treated ratification as contingent on Protocol amendment with binding enforcement language—'no text by Wednesday, deal dies' was the central frame throughout.
